limitations: Possible significant references were not discovered, including "grey literature".
The modality of the stimuli used (unimodality, e.g., visual domain only) reduces the richness of the experience.
The aspects studied are fundamentally limited to beauty and pleasure, which are not sufficient.
Difficulty of explaining experiences in exclusively physiological terms (neurology-experience relationship).
A brain area can be related to several processes, making invalid inferences.
The number of aspects that influence artistic and aesthetic experiences is limited.
Procedural conflicts (ceteris paribus logic sacrifices complexity, rigidity of neuroimaging protocols, laboratory context alters results).
Multiple cognitive-emotional processes involved do not occur simultaneously, misaligning causal assignment of recordings.
Technical restrictions associated with neurophysiological recording technologies (e.g., immobility of fMRI).
Lack of a commonly accepted methodology, obstructing understanding between research groups and comparability of results.
Results are difficult to extrapolate into design guidelines for practical application in architecture.
It is not possible to liken architecture to the artistic-aesthetic (depth of architectural function).
The experience of architecture is not one-off; it is an experiential continuum.
Fragmentation of the cognitive-emotional dimension of architecture encourages the tendency toward case studies.
Limited understanding of what affects the sense of presence.
The analysis of neurophysiological data is challenging.
Neurophysiological indices for cognitive-emotional dimension of architecture are not yet fully developed and available for academic/professional use.
